stimulus.text:
United States military occupations in Latin America came to an end in the 1930s.

| Country | Year the last United States Marines left |
| Nicaragua | 1933 |
| Haiti | 1934 |

Paraphrase: At the Inter-American Conference in Montevideo, Uruguay, in December 1933, Secretary of State Cordell Hull signed a declaration that no nation has the right to interfere in the internal or external affairs of another nation.
stimulus.source_note: Occupation end years from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.11, and Princeton Review, Chapter 11. Montevideo declaration paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.11.

source: original; table from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.11, and Princeton Review, Chapter 11; Montevideo declaration paraphrased from Barron's
stem: The actions in the table and the Montevideo declaration best illustrate which of the following?

options.text: A return to the Roosevelt Corollary
options.misconception: The Roosevelt Corollary claimed a right to intervene; the Good Neighbor Policy gave that up.

options.text: A new American empire in South America
options.misconception: The United States was leaving countries, not building an empire there.

options.text: A decision to annex Latin American territory
options.misconception: No territory was annexed; Marines were withdrawn.

options.text: A break with intervention in Latin America

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 claimed an American right to police the hemisphere.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the occupations ended in 1933 and 1934, and no new ones replaced them.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the United States signed a declaration against interfering in other nations' affairs.
rationales.D: Withdrawing the Marines and signing the Montevideo declaration reversed three decades of intervention.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows the last Marines leaving Nicaragua in 1933 and Haiti in 1934.
2. At Montevideo in 1933 Secretary Hull signed a declaration against interfering in any nation's affairs.
3. In 1934 Roosevelt also repealed the Platt Amendment, which had let the United States intervene in Cuba.
4. Together these steps break with the Roosevelt Corollary, which had claimed a right to intervene.
Remember: ending occupations and signing non-intervention are the marks of a policy change.
